14707:
The prewrath view holds that the church will go through the first part of Daniel's seventieth week, including the great tribulation, the persecution of believers by antichrist that begins at the midpoint. That persecution will be cut short by the coming of Christ, announced by cosmic signs in the sun, moon and stars. At that coming the church is raptured, and immediately afterward God's wrath, the day of the Lord, is poured out on the world through the trumpet and bowl judgments, before Christ's final victory at the end of the week.

The key distinction is between the wrath of Satan and antichrist against the saints, which believers may endure, and the wrath of God, from which believers are promised deliverance. Prewrath advocates usually place the rapture at the sixth seal of Revelation, before the seventh seal opens the trumpet judgments.

14773:
Posttribulationism holds that the rapture and the second coming are a single event occurring after the tribulation. The church will be present through the final period of distress and the career of antichrist, preserved by God through it, and at Christ's visible return believers who have died will be raised and living believers transformed and caught up to meet him in the air, accompanying him as he comes to earth to reign.

Posttribulationists are premillennial; they expect Christ's earthly reign to follow his return. They stress that the church has always been called to endure tribulation, that the New Testament uses the same terms for Christ's coming in rapture and return passages, and that believers are protected from God's wrath without being removed from the world.

14836:
Most Christians in history, including Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and most other Protestant traditions, have read 1 Thess 4:13-18 not as a separate rapture event but as a description of the one second coming of Christ at the end of history. When Christ returns visibly, the dead are raised, living believers are transformed and gathered to him, and the general resurrection and final judgment follow, leading to the new heavens and new earth.

This view is held by amillennialists, postmillennialists and partial preterists, who do not expect a future seven-year tribulation followed by an earthly millennium. It shares with posttribulationism the conviction that believers are gathered at the single visible return, but differs in seeing no subsequent earthly kingdom. Full preterists also deny a separate rapture but place the coming in AD 70.
